screens.title: Primitive Obsession & Replace Type Code with Class/Subclasses
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will explore a common code smell called Primitive Obsession — the habit of using raw primitives like strings or integers to represent important domain concepts. We'll learn why this pattern weakens type safety and scatters behavior across conditionals, and how two refactorings — Replace Type Code with Class and Replace Type Code with Subclasses — restore clarity and encapsulation. You will see concrete Python examples: an Account example that moves a primitive account type into an AccountType object, and a Product status exercise where a string status is refactored into an abstract ProductStatus with subclasses. These refactorings let your code express intent, centralize behavior, and make future extensions safer and easier. Along the way we'll highlight common pitfalls, like over-engineering with needless subclasses or creating anemic objects that only hold data. By the end, you'll be ready to spot type-code smells in your own codebase and choose the right refactoring path. Consider an example from your project now: is there a string or integer acting like a tiny domain object? That is often the place to begin.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Primitive Obsession

Primitive Obsession

Why using raw primitives for meaningful types hides intent and spreads conditional logic across your code.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
Identify Primitive Obsession and refactor type codes into classes and subclasses.
Live coding
Step-by-step Python refactor of Product status from string to polymorphic classes.
Why it matters
Better type safety, centralized behavior, fewer conditionals, and easier extensions.
Preview: Account example
class Account:
  CHECKING = 0
  SAVINGS = 1
  LOAN = 2

  def __init__(self, account_id, balance, account_type):
    self.account_id = account_id
    self.balance = balance
    self.account_type = account_type

  def get_interest_rate(self):
    if self.account_type == Account.CHECKING:
      return 0.01
    elif self.account_type == Account.SAVINGS:
      return 0.02
    elif self.account_type == Account.LOAN:
      return 0.05
Key takeaway
If a primitive is carrying domain behavior, it likely belongs to a class or subclass.
Explore Key Topics
What we'll cover in this chapter
Primitive Obsession
Recognize when primitives stand in for domain objects and how that hides intent.
Replace Type Code with Class
Turn a type code into a small object with data and behavior.
Replace with Subclasses
Use subclasses when types have distinct behavior; embrace polymorphism.
Tip: As you watch the live-coding demo, listen for conditional logic you can move into a single class or into subclasses. Ask: does a type variation change behavior or just data?

For each refactoring objective, you should be able to run unit tests that assert behavior before and after the change. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Verification

Proof of correctness

Testing and migration steps after refactoring.

  • Write unit tests that assert behavior for each type before refactoring and after — behavior must match.
  • Check that conditionals checking type codes are removed or reduced in client classes.
  • Update serialization and database mapping code to persist the new objects or subclass discriminators.
  • Run integration tests to ensure factories and creation flows still produce correct runtime objects.

Common pitfalls

Anemic type objects: They hold data but leave all behavior in conditionals elsewhere. The goal is to move behavior in.
Premature subclasses: Only use them when behaviors truly diverge, otherwise prefer a single richer type object.
Persistence mismatch: Make sure database schemas and serializers are updated to accept new objects or discriminators.

screens.title: What is Primitive Obsession?
screens.narratorSegment: Primitive Obsession is a design smell where primitive data types are used to represent meaningful domain concepts. For example, storing money as a float and currency as a string, or using integers for order statuses, means your types carry no behavior and no validation. This creates code that is less expressive and more error-prone. A concrete example is using an integer for an account type: zero for checking, one for savings, and two for loan. That single integer doesn't prevent you from passing it to unrelated functions, nor does it encapsulate rules like whether deposits are allowed. A common misconception is that primitives are always simpler; they are simple to write but impose cognitive load when behavior spans the system. When you replace a type code with an object, you make the code self-documenting and you create a natural place for validation and behavior. To check your understanding, scan a small module in your codebase for repeated comparisons to the same integer or string. If you find many checks, that is a likely symptom. The takeaway: primitives are fine for raw values, but once a primitive represents a domain concept and behavior, model it explicitly.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Definition

Primitive Obsession

A primitive value used everywhere to indicate a concept that deserves its own model.

Example: An account_type integer used in many if/elif blocks. The integer alone doesn't convey rules like whether deposits are allowed.
Why it matters: primitives lack behavior, validation, and clear intent. They cause scattered conditional logic and fragile changes.
Misconception: Primitives are always simpler. Reality: they are simple initially but increase maintenance costs as behavior grows.
Key Takeaway

If a value has behavior, validation, or domain meaning beyond storage, model it as an object.

Quick diagnostic
  1. Find repeated checks like status == "X" or type == 2.
  2. Look for scattered formatting or validation for the same primitive.
  3. Count the number of places that interpret the same primitive; many places indicate a smell.
Reflection
Name one primitive in your code that acts like a tiny object. That is your candidate for refactoring.

screens.title: Problems caused by Primitive Obsession
screens.narratorSegment: Primitive Obsession causes three tightly related problems. First, type safety and expressiveness suffer: when you use a raw float or string for a domain concept, nothing prevents that value from being misused or combined with unrelated values. For example, adding a weight value to a money amount is syntactically possible but semantically wrong. Second, behavior is scattered: formatting, validation, or state transitions for that concept are implemented in many places, increasing duplication and the risk of inconsistent behavior. Third, conditional complexity grows: clients use lengthy if/elif/else or switch statements to branch on a primitive type code, which violates the Open/Closed Principle because adding a new type forces changes across many blocks. A common misconception is conflating enums and full objects — an enum is sometimes sufficient for fixed, simple categories, but when behavior or validation is required, an object or subclasses are better. Use the following process: spot the smell, extract a small class to encapsulate data and behavior, run tests, and only escalate to subclasses when behavioral divergence demands it. That orderly process keeps refactors safe and incremental. Problems caused by Primitive Obsession means primitive obsession reduces type safety, scatters behavior, and creates conditional explosion that resists extension.. In practical terms, type safety loss, scattered behavior, conditional complexity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Process Flow

Why it becomes a maintenance problem

Type safety is lost: primitives don't prevent misuse and don't convey intent to readers or tools.
Behavior is scattered: formatting, validation, and transitions are duplicated and inconsistent.
Conditional complexity grows: if/elif blocks proliferate and violate Open/Closed Principle.
Misconception: Enums always solve this. Enums help naming but don't hold behavior; prefer objects when logic belongs with the type.

Refactoring process

1
Identify repeated checks for the same primitive or duplicated formatting/validation logic.
2
Extract a small class to hold the type information and any related behavior.
3
Run tests, update persistence layers if needed, and confirm reductions in conditional logic.
4
If behavior splits significantly, convert to subclasses to use polymorphism.

screens.title: Replace Type Code with Class — Account example
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through the Replace Type Code with Class refactoring using the Account example. Initially, the Account class stores an integer account_type and uses if/elif statements to compute interest rates and deposit rules. The concept of account type is a domain object: it carries a name, an interest rate, and whether deposits are allowed. Replacing the integer with an AccountType object centralizes these properties and removes conditional logic from Account. The refactored Account holds an AccountType instance and delegates get_interest_rate and deposit behavior to that object. A common misconception is thinking this adds boilerplate. In practice, it reduces duplicated branches and makes client code clearer: the Account class no longer needs to know the numeric codes. To verify the change, write tests that assert interest rates before and after the refactor and confirm deposit behavior matches the original rules. The key benefit is delegation: behavior travels with the type it belongs to, making future changes localized. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Replace Type Code with Class
Original snippet (uses integer type codes)
class Account:
  CHECKING = 0
  SAVINGS = 1
  LOAN = 2

  def __init__(self, account_id, balance, account_type):
    self.account_id = account_id
    self.balance = balance
    self.account_type = account_type

  def get_interest_rate(self):
    if self.account_type == Account.CHECKING:
      return 0.01
    elif self.account_type == Account.SAVINGS:
      return 0.02
    elif self.account_type == Account.LOAN:
      return 0.05

  def deposit(self, amount):
    if self.account_type == Account.LOAN:
      print("Cannot deposit directly into a loan account.")
      return False
    self.balance += amount
    return True
Refactored: AccountType as a small data object with behavior
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AccountType:
  name: str
  interest_rate: float
  can_deposit: bool

class AccountTypes:
  CHECKING = AccountType("Checking", 0.01, True)
  SAVINGS = AccountType("Savings", 0.02, True)
  LOAN = AccountType("Loan", 0.05, False)

class Account:
  def __init__(self, account_id, balance, account_type: AccountType):
    self.account_id = account_id
    self.balance = balance
    self.account_type = account_type

  def get_interest_rate(self):
    return self.account_type.interest_rate

  def deposit(self, amount):
    if not self.account_type.can_deposit:
      print(f"Cannot deposit directly into a {self.account_type.name} account.")
      return False
    self.balance += amount
    return True
Concrete example
An Account now holds an AccountType with an interest rate and deposit rule. The Account delegates logic and avoids numeric checks.
Key Takeaway

Small type objects encapsulate rules and make client classes simpler.

screens.title: Replace Type Code with Subclasses — When to use subclasses
screens.narratorSegment: Subclasses are appropriate when different type codes imply significantly different behavior or state that can't be cleanly expressed by a simple data object. In our account example, if checking, savings, and loan accounts require different deposit rules, interest calculations with additional state, or specialized methods, modeling them as distinct subclasses of a BaseAccount class lets each account implement its own behavior. This removes conditionals entirely: client code can call the same methods and rely on polymorphism to dispatch the right behavior. A practical misconception is to use subclasses for minor differences like a single flag; these cases often benefit from an AccountType object instead. Subclassing increases the number of classes and can complicate persistence. Use it when behavior diverges and the Open/Closed Principle matters: adding a new type means adding a new subclass rather than scattering if/else changes. The architecture becomes cleaner because behavior is placed where it belongs and client code becomes simpler and more robust. Replace Type Code with Subclasses — When to use subclasses means choose subclasses when different types have significantly different behaviors and states that polymorphism can encapsulate.. In practical terms, escalate to subclasses when behavior diverges. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Subclasses

Architecture: BaseAccount with subclasses

Each subclass implements type-specific behavior, eliminating conditionals.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class BaseAccount(ABC):
  def __init__(self, account_id, balance):
    self.account_id = account_id
    self.balance = balance

  @abstractmethod
  def get_interest_rate(self):
    pass

  @abstractmethod
  def deposit(self, amount):
    pass

class CheckingAccount(BaseAccount):
  def get_interest_rate(self):
    return 0.01
  def deposit(self, amount):
    self.balance += amount
    return True

class LoanAccount(BaseAccount):
  def get_interest_rate(self):
    return 0.05
  def deposit(self, amount):
    print("Use make_payment instead.")
    return False

When subclasses are overkill

If variations are only configuration values like an interest rate or a single flag, prefer a type object.
If persistence becomes complex because of many subclasses, weigh the maintenance cost against behavioral clarity.
Use factories to centralize creation and to keep client code decoupled from concrete classes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Product — Before
Original Product class using status strings and conditionals
class Product:
  def __init__(self, product_id, name, price, status: str):
    self.product_id = product_id
    self.name = name
    self.price = price
    self.status = status  # "IN_STOCK", "OUT_OF_STOCK", "DISCONTINUED"

  def is_available_for_purchase(self):
    if self.status == "IN_STOCK":
      return True
    elif self.status == "OUT_OF_STOCK":
      return False
    elif self.status == "DISCONTINUED":
      return False
    else:
      print(f"Warning: Unknown status '{self.status}' for product {self.product_id}.")
      return False

  def get_display_message(self):
    if self.status == "IN_STOCK":
      return "Available for immediate purchase."
    elif self.status == "OUT_OF_STOCK":
      return "Currently out of stock. Check back soon."
    elif self.status == "DISCONTINUED":
      return "This product is no longer available."
    else:
      return "Status unknown."
Quick analysis
  • Many places check the same status strings.
  • Adding a new status requires updating every conditional block.
  • Messages and availability behavior are scattered inside Product.

screens.title: Introduce ProductStatus base class
screens.narratorSegment: To remove conditionals we introduce an abstract ProductStatus base class that defines the interface for statuses: methods like is_available_for_purchase and get_display_message. This claim means every concrete status class must implement those methods. A concrete example is InStockStatus returning True for availability and a friendly message, while DiscontinuedStatus returns False and an archival message. Defining a base class clarifies the contract and enables polymorphism. Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Subclasses & Factory
Concrete subclasses implement behavior directly
class InStockStatus(ProductStatus):
  def is_available_for_purchase(self):
    return True
  def get_display_message(self):
    return "Available for immediate purchase."

class OutOfStockStatus(ProductStatus):
  def is_available_for_purchase(self):
    return False
  def get_display_message(self):
    return "Currently out of stock. Check back soon."

class DiscontinuedStatus(ProductStatus):
  def is_available_for_purchase(self):
    return False
  def get_display_message(self):
    return "This product is no longer available."

class ProductStatusFactory:
  @staticmethod
  def from_status_string(status_str):
    if status_str == "IN_STOCK":
      return InStockStatus()
    elif status_str == "OUT_OF_STOCK":
      return OutOfStockStatus()
    elif status_str == "DISCONTINUED":
      return DiscontinuedStatus()
    else:
      raise ValueError(f"Unknown status: {status_str}")
Notes
  • Factory centralizes mapping from strings to classes, easing changes to persistence.
  • Tests should instantiate each subclass directly and via the factory.

screens.title: Class vs Subclasses — Choosing the right refactor
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between a single type class and a subclass hierarchy is a practical judgment. Use a simple class when the type mainly carries data and one or two small behaviors: a single object with fields and a couple of methods often eliminates most conditional logic with minimal complexity. Use subclasses when behaviors diverge significantly — for example, when methods have different algorithms, additional state, or side effects per type. The Account example shows a case where a simple AccountType object suffices if only the interest rate and a deposit flag differ. Conversely, when accounts require different deposit workflows or additional methods like make_payment on loans, subclasses are cleaner. A common misconception is that subclasses always offer better design; they add complexity and may complicate persistence and testing. When in doubt, start with a small type object, add behavior to it, and only extract subclasses when you see duplicated method logic across multiple type objects. This incremental approach preserves simplicity while enabling extension. screens.title: Common mistakes, persistence, and testing
screens.narratorSegment: After refactoring, be mindful of a few safety concerns. First, avoid creating anemic type objects that only hold data but leave behavior in conditionals elsewhere; the goal is to move logic into the type so conditionals disappear. Second, persistence: when you replace primitives with objects or subclasses you must update serialization and database mappings. For example, store a simple status identifier and reconstruct the status object at load time, or implement custom serializers that convert to and from the persisted representation. Third, client code changes: all places that previously referenced raw primitives must be updated to use the new object A P I or factory. Testing is critical: write unit tests for each new type object or subclass and regression tests for the refactored client classes. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will explore a common code smell called Primitive Obsession — the habit of using raw primitives like strings or integers to represent important domain concepts. We'll learn why this pattern weakens type safety and scatters behavior across conditionals, and how two refactorings — Replace Type Code with Class and Replace Type Code with Subclasses — restore clarity and encapsulation. You will see concrete Python examples: an Account example that moves a primitive account type into an AccountType object, and a Product status exercise where a string status is refactored into an abstract ProductStatus with subclasses. These refactorings let your code express intent, centralize behavior, and make future extensions safer and easier. Along the way we'll highlight common pitfalls, like over-engineering with needless subclasses or creating anemic objects that only hold data. By the end, you'll be ready to spot type-code smells in your own codebase and choose the right refactoring path. Consider an example from your project now: is there a string or integer acting like a tiny domain object? That is often the place to begin.

By the end of these screens you should be able to identify Primitive Obsession, explain why it weakens code, and apply two focused refactorings. First, you will learn to spot type codes: integers or strings that silently represent a domain concept. Then you will practice replacing those codes with a small class that encapsulates intent and simple behavior. Next, you will learn when to escalate to subclasses so that each type implements its own behavior polymorphically. Finally, you'll evaluate trade-offs: when a class is enough versus when a hierarchy pays off, and how to avoid common mistakes like anemic objects or premature subclassing. Each objective includes a short example and a verification milestone so you can test your competency. These skills will make your code easier to read, safer to change, and more extensible, because behavior travels with the data it belongs to rather than being scattered behind conditionals.

This screen explains how to verify your work and what common pitfalls to check after refactoring. For each refactoring objective, you should be able to run unit tests that assert behavior before and after the change. For Replace Type Code with Class, tests should confirm that behavior delegated to the new class returns the same results and that client code no longer contains type-check conditionals. For Replace Type Code with Subclasses, tests should cover each subclass's behavior and confirm the factory or creation path returns the correct concrete class. Watch for common mistakes: creating an object that only holds data but doesn't reduce conditionals, or prematurely introducing subclass complexity when a data-rich object would suffice. Also verify persistence: serialization and database mappings may need updates. Finally, ensure client code compiles and that errors for unknown codes surface early. These verification steps help you keep refactors safe and incremental.

Primitive Obsession is a design smell where primitive data types are used to represent meaningful domain concepts. For example, storing money as a float and currency as a string, or using integers for order statuses, means your types carry no behavior and no validation. This creates code that is less expressive and more error-prone. A concrete example is using an integer for an account type: zero for checking, one for savings, and two for loan. That single integer doesn't prevent you from passing it to unrelated functions, nor does it encapsulate rules like whether deposits are allowed. A common misconception is that primitives are always simpler; they are simple to write but impose cognitive load when behavior spans the system. When you replace a type code with an object, you make the code self-documenting and you create a natural place for validation and behavior. To check your understanding, scan a small module in your codebase for repeated comparisons to the same integer or string. If you find many checks, that is a likely symptom. The takeaway: primitives are fine for raw values, but once a primitive represents a domain concept and behavior, model it explicitly.

Primitive Obsession causes three tightly related problems. First, type safety and expressiveness suffer: when you use a raw float or string for a domain concept, nothing prevents that value from being misused or combined with unrelated values. For example, adding a weight value to a money amount is syntactically possible but semantically wrong. Second, behavior is scattered: formatting, validation, or state transitions for that concept are implemented in many places, increasing duplication and the risk of inconsistent behavior. Third, conditional complexity grows: clients use lengthy if/elif/else or switch statements to branch on a primitive type code, which violates the Open/Closed Principle because adding a new type forces changes across many blocks. A common misconception is conflating enums and full objects — an enum is sometimes sufficient for fixed, simple categories, but when behavior or validation is required, an object or subclasses are better. Use the following process: spot the smell, extract a small class to encapsulate data and behavior, run tests, and only escalate to subclasses when behavioral divergence demands it. That orderly process keeps refactors safe and incremental. Problems caused by Primitive Obsession means primitive obsession reduces type safety, scatters behavior, and creates conditional explosion that resists extension.. In practical terms, type safety loss, scattered behavior, conditional complexity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This lesson walks through the Replace Type Code with Class refactoring using the Account example. Initially, the Account class stores an integer account_type and uses if/elif statements to compute interest rates and deposit rules. The concept of account type is a domain object: it carries a name, an interest rate, and whether deposits are allowed. Replacing the integer with an AccountType object centralizes these properties and removes conditional logic from Account. The refactored Account holds an AccountType instance and delegates get_interest_rate and deposit behavior to that object. A common misconception is thinking this adds boilerplate. In practice, it reduces duplicated branches and makes client code clearer: the Account class no longer needs to know the numeric codes. To verify the change, write tests that assert interest rates before and after the refactor and confirm deposit behavior matches the original rules. The key benefit is delegation: behavior travels with the type it belongs to, making future changes localized. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Subclasses are appropriate when different type codes imply significantly different behavior or state that can't be cleanly expressed by a simple data object. In our account example, if checking, savings, and loan accounts require different deposit rules, interest calculations with additional state, or specialized methods, modeling them as distinct subclasses of a BaseAccount class lets each account implement its own behavior. This removes conditionals entirely: client code can call the same methods and rely on polymorphism to dispatch the right behavior. A practical misconception is to use subclasses for minor differences like a single flag; these cases often benefit from an AccountType object instead. Subclassing increases the number of classes and can complicate persistence. Use it when behavior diverges and the Open/Closed Principle matters: adding a new type means adding a new subclass rather than scattering if/else changes. The architecture becomes cleaner because behavior is placed where it belongs and client code becomes simpler and more robust. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We now move to the hands-on product status example. The initial Product class stores a string status with values like IN_STOCK, OUT_OF_STOCK, or DISCONTINUED. Its methods check the string in if/elif blocks to determine availability and display messages. This is a classic type-code smell: the status string carries domain meaning and behavior, but it's not modeled as an object. A concrete example: is_available_for_purchase returns True only for the IN_STOCK string, and get_display_message returns different messages depending on the string. A misconception is thinking that strings are easier to serialize or store — while they are easy to persist, the maintenance cost occurs when you need to add behavior or a new status because you must modify every conditional. As a diagnostic, search your codebase for repeated string comparisons to the same status; each occurrence is a place to move behavior into a status object or subclass. Choosing between a single type class and a subclass hierarchy is a practical judgment. Use a simple class when the type mainly carries data and one or two small behaviors: a single object with fields and a couple of methods often eliminates most conditional logic with minimal complexity. Use subclasses when behaviors diverge significantly — for example, when methods have different algorithms, additional state, or side effects per type. The Account example shows a case where a simple AccountType object suffices if only the interest rate and a deposit flag differ. Let's summarize the essential ideas you should carry forward. First, Primitive Obsession is when primitives are used to represent domain concepts; this causes reduced type safety and scattered behavior. Second, Replace Type Code with Class is the low-friction refactor: extract a small object that encapsulates the data and small behaviors, reducing conditionals and improving clarity. Third, Replace Type Code with Subclasses uses polymorphism to move significantly different behaviors into concrete classes, supporting the Open/Closed Principle. Remember the practical trade-offs: prefer the simplest change that removes duplication, update persistence and tests, and avoid anemic objects or premature subclassing. When in doubt, start with a type object, add behavior to it, and escalate to subclasses only after behavior diverges. These steps will make your codebase clearer to readers and safer to extend.
